nodes.label: Mubarak
nodes.full: Hosni Mubarak, a former air force commander who became president on the assassination of Sadat in October 1981, was re-elected through referendums and, from 2005, contested elections until the uprising of January–February 2011; he resigned and handed power to the army's supreme council on 11 February 2011, was tried and, after a long legal process, saw the charges of complicity in the killing of protesters dismissed in November 2014 after a retrial, served a sentence for embezzlement and died in February 2020.
nodes.src: Egypt 1952–today folio; Joshua Stacher, Adaptable Autocrats (2012); Egyptian court rulings (2012–2015).

nodes.label: Sisi
nodes.full: Field Marshal Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, minister of defence under President Mohamed Morsi, announced on 3 July 2013, after large demonstrations, the removal of Morsi, whom his supporters called the victim of a coup and his opponents the fulfilment of a popular revolution; he was elected president in 2014, re-elected in 2018 and 2023, and the constitutional amendments of 2019 allow him to remain until 2030.
nodes.src: Egypt 1952–today folio; Constitution of Egypt (2014, amended 2019); Egyptian National Election Authority results.

nodes.label: Bashar al-Assad
nodes.full: Bashar al-Assad, an ophthalmologist who succeeded his father Hafez as president in June 2000 after a constitutional amendment lowered the age of eligibility, ruled Syria through the uprising and civil war of 2011 to 2024, with the help of Iran, Hezbollah and Russia, until an offensive by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham and allied groups reached Damascus on 8 December 2024; he fled to Russia, which granted him asylum, ending the family's rule of more than fifty years.
nodes.src: Syria 1946–today folio; Lisa Wedeen, Ambiguities of Domination (1999); Reuters and AP reports (8 December 2024).

nodes.label: Ahmed al-Sharaa
nodes.full: Ahmed al-Sharaa, formerly known by the nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Jolani and leader of Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, which had once been affiliated with al-Qaeda, led the offensive that ended the Assad government and was declared interim president of Syria by a gathering of armed factions on 29 January 2025; a constitutional declaration of March 2025 set a five-year transition, indirect parliamentary elections took place in October 2025, and as of October 2026 the new authorities have been recognised by many states but face disputes with the Kurdish-led forces, the Druze and Alawite communities and Israel.
nodes.src: Constitutional Declaration of the Syrian Arab Republic (13 March 2025); Syria 1946–today folio; Reuters, AP and Al Jazeera reports.

nodes.label: Erdoğan
nodes.full: Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, a former mayor of Istanbul and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AKP), which won the election of November 2002, was prime minister from 2003 to 2014, president from August 2014 and, after the referendum of April 2017, head of an executive presidency from 2018, re-elected in the run-off of 28 May 2023; his supporters point to the economic growth, infrastructure and the end of military tutelage, his critics to the concentration of power, the purge after 2016 and the jailing of opponents.
nodes.src: Turkey 1980–today folio; Soner Çağaptay, The New Sultan (2017); Supreme Election Council results (2023).

nodes.label: Khamenei and his successor
nodes.full: Ali Khamenei, who became Supreme Leader on Khomeini's death in 1989, held the office through the presidencies of Rafsanjani, Khatami, Ahmadinejad, Rouhani, Raisi and Pezeshkian and was reported killed in the American and Israeli strikes that opened the war of 28 February 2026; the Assembly of Experts named his son Mojtaba Khamenei as successor in March 2026, a succession that critics compared to a hereditary one and that, as of October 2026, takes place in conditions of war and sanctions.
nodes.src: Iran 1979–today folio; Iranian state media reports (28 February–March 2026); Britannica and Reuters coverage of the 2026 war.

nodes.label: Mohammed bin Salman
nodes.full: Mohammed bin Salman, the son of King Salman, became defence minister in January 2015, crown prince in June 2017 in place of his cousin Muhammad bin Nayef and prime minister in September 2022; he has led the Vision 2030 programme of economic and social change, the war in Yemen from 2015, the detentions at the Ritz-Carlton in November 2017 and an assertive foreign policy, and the American intelligence assessment attributes to him the approval of the killing of Jamal Khashoggi in October 2018, which he has denied ordering while accepting responsibility as leader.
nodes.src: Saudi 1902–today folio; US Office of the Director of National Intelligence report (February 2021); Ben Hubbard, MBS (2020).

nodes.label: Netanyahu
nodes.full: Benjamin Netanyahu, leader of the Likud, has been Israel's prime minister in 1996–1999, 2009–2021 and since December 2022, the longest-serving in the country's history, through the Oslo years, the Gaza wars, the judicial reform conflict of 2023 and the war that followed the attack of 7 October 2023; he stands trial on charges of bribery and breach of trust, which he denies, and the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant against him in November 2024, which Israel rejects as illegitimate.
nodes.src: Israel 1948–today folio; ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I decision (21 November 2024); Israeli District Court indictment (2019, trial from 2020).

nodes.label: Abbas and the Palestinian Authority
nodes.full: Mahmoud Abbas, long the PLO's negotiator, succeeded Yasser Arafat as chairman of the PLO after Arafat's death on 11 November 2004 and was elected president of the Palestinian Authority in January 2005; Hamas won the legislative elections of January 2006 and, after a short civil conflict, took over Gaza in June 2007, leaving the Authority governing parts of the West Bank, and, by reports to 2026, no presidential or parliamentary elections have been held since, so that his mandate is disputed by Hamas and other opponents.
nodes.src: Palestine 1948–today folio; Central Elections Commission (Palestine) records; Khalidi, The Hundred Years' War on Palestine (2020).

nodes.label: Iraqi prime ministers
nodes.full: The prime ministers of the Iraq of the constitution of 2005 were chosen in each case through a negotiation among the main sectarian and ethnic blocs: Ibrahim al-Jaafari, Nouri al-Maliki (2006–2014), Haider al-Abadi, Adel Abdul-Mahdi, Mustafa al-Kadhimi, Mohammed Shia al-Sudani (2022–2026) and, after the elections of November 2025 and a long process of coalition bargaining, Ali al-Zaidi, whose parliament approved a partial cabinet in May 2026.
nodes.src: Iraq 2003–today folio; Al Jazeera and Reuters reports (14 May 2026); Toby Dodge, Iraq: From War to a New Authoritarianism (2012).

nodes.label: Invasion of Kuwait and the Gulf War
nodes.full: Iraq invaded and annexed Kuwait on 2 August 1990 over debt, oil and an old territorial claim; a coalition of some thirty-five states under the United States, acting under Security Council resolution 678, began an air campaign on 17 January 1991 and a ground offensive on 24 February that freed Kuwait within a hundred hours, with perhaps 20,000 to 35,000 Iraqi military dead by various estimates and some 300 coalition dead; the Shia and Kurdish uprisings that followed were crushed.
nodes.src: UN Security Council resolution 678 (1990); Lawrence Freedman and Efraim Karsh, The Gulf Conflict (1993); Iraq 1979–2003 folio.

nodes.label: Second Intifada
nodes.full: After the failure of the Camp David talks of July 2000 and Ariel Sharon's visit to the Haram al-Sharif on 28 September, violence began that included Palestinian suicide bombings in Israeli cities and Israeli operations such as Defensive Shield in 2002, the reoccupation of the West Bank towns and the separation barrier; some 3,000 to 3,300 Palestinians and about 1,000 Israelis were killed by 2005, and Israel withdrew from Gaza in the disengagement of August–September 2005.
nodes.src: B'Tselem statistics; Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs data; Palestine 1948–today and Israel 1948–today folios.

nodes.label: Lebanon War of 2006
nodes.full: Hezbollah's capture of two Israeli soldiers in a raid across the border on 12 July 2006 led to a thirty-four-day war in which Israel bombed Lebanon's infrastructure and Beirut's southern suburbs and Hezbollah fired some 4,000 rockets into northern Israel; some 1,100 to 1,200 Lebanese, most of them civilians, and about 160 Israelis, mostly soldiers, died, and Security Council resolution 1701 ended the fighting.
nodes.src: UN Security Council resolution 1701 (2006); Human Rights Watch, Why They Died (2007); Winograd Commission report (2008).

nodes.label: Invasion of Iraq
nodes.full: The United States, Britain and allies invaded Iraq on 20 March 2003 on the stated grounds of weapons of mass destruction, which were not found, without a Security Council authorisation; Baghdad fell on 9 April, Saddam Hussein was captured in December and hanged in December 2006, and the dissolution of the army and the de-Ba'thification, followed by insurgency and sectarian war, led to estimates of Iraqi deaths ranging from some 150,000 to several hundred thousand and some 4,500 American dead before the American withdrawal of December 2011.
nodes.src: Thomas Ricks, Fiasco (2006); Iraq Body Count; Charles Tripp, A History of Iraq (2007); Iraq 2003–today folio.

nodes.label: Islamic State
nodes.full: The Islamic State of Iraq and Syria, a successor of al-Qaeda in Iraq, took Mosul on 10 June 2014 and proclaimed a caliphate under Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi on 29 June, ruling at its height some 8 million people with a regime of enslavement of the Yazidis, public executions and taxation; the coalition and local forces retook Mosul in July 2017, Raqqa in October 2017 and the last village, Baghuz, in March 2019, at the cost of tens of thousands of lives and the destruction of the old city of Mosul.
nodes.src: Fawaz Gerges, ISIS: A History (2016); Patrick Cockburn, The Rise of Islamic State (2015); Iraq 2003–today and Syria folios.

nodes.label: Syrian civil war
nodes.full: Protests of March 2011 against the Assad government were met with force and became an armed conflict among the government and its allies, a mixed opposition, jihadist groups, the Islamic State and Kurdish-led forces, with the use of chemical weapons (Ghouta, 21 August 2013), sieges and barrel bombs, foreign intervention by Iran, Russia, Turkey and the United States, and some 6 million refugees and 7 million displaced inside the country; the United Nations documented more than 300,000 civilian deaths to 2021 and monitors give higher estimates.
nodes.src: UN OHCHR, Update on Civilian Deaths in Syria (2022); UNHCR figures; Syria 1946–today folio; Charles Lister, The Syrian Jihad (2015).

nodes.label: Egyptian revolution
nodes.full: Mass demonstrations beginning on 25 January 2011, the Day of Anger, and the occupation of Tahrir Square brought down Mubarak in eighteen days, with some 840 dead by the report of the fact-finding commission; free elections brought the Muslim Brotherhood's Morsi to the presidency in June 2012, and after the removal of Morsi on 3 July 2013 the security forces dispersed the sit-ins at Rabaa and al-Nahda on 14 August, killing at least 600 and by the count of Human Rights Watch at least 817 people.
nodes.src: Egyptian fact-finding commission report (2011); Human Rights Watch, All According to Plan (2014); Egypt 1952–today folio.

nodes.label: War in Yemen
nodes.full: After the Houthi movement took Sanaa on 21 September 2014 and advanced on Aden, a coalition under Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates intervened on 26 March 2015 to restore President Hadi; the war, with air strikes, a blockade, famine conditions and the fragmentation of the south, killed, by a United Nations Development Programme estimate, some 377,000 people to the end of 2021, about 60 per cent by indirect causes, and the truce of April 2022 has held in part, while the Houthis' attacks on shipping from late 2023 widened the conflict.
nodes.src: UNDP, Assessing the Impact of War in Yemen (2021); Yemen 1900–today folio; UN Panel of Experts reports.

nodes.label: 7 October and the Gaza War
nodes.full: Hamas and allied groups attacked Israeli communities and a music festival on 7 October 2023, killing some 1,200 people, most of them civilians, and taking about 250 hostages; Israel's air and ground campaign in Gaza that followed killed, according to the Gaza health ministry, more than 73,000 people by September 2026, a figure the United Nations regards as broadly reliable though Israel disputes it and says many of the dead were combatants, and displaced most of the population; a ceasefire took effect on 10 October 2025, under which the living hostages were released, though strikes and disputes over disarmament, withdrawal and reconstruction continue as of October 2026.
nodes.src: Gaza Ministry of Health figures (September 2026); Israeli government figures on 7 October; UN OCHA reports; Palestine and Israel 1948–today folios.

nodes.label: Israel–Hezbollah war
nodes.full: Hezbollah began firing on northern Israel on 8 October 2023 in support of Hamas; the exchange of fire, the evacuation of border communities on both sides, the explosion of its members' pagers on 17–18 September 2024, the killing of its secretary-general Hassan Nasrallah on 27 September and the Israeli ground incursion ended in a ceasefire on 27 November 2024, and Israel kept positions in southern Lebanon; in 2026, during the war with Iran, fighting there was reported to have resumed.
nodes.src: Lebanon 1943–today folio; US-brokered ceasefire arrangement (27 November 2024); Reuters and AP reports.

nodes.label: Twelve-Day War
nodes.full: Israel opened an air campaign against Iran's nuclear and military sites and commanders on 13 June 2025, Iran replied with missiles and drones, and on 22 June the United States struck the enrichment plants at Fordow and Natanz and the site at Isfahan; the ceasefire of 24 June followed, with some 600 to 1,100 dead in Iran, depending on the source, and some 28 to 32 killed in Israel.
nodes.src: Iranian judiciary and health ministry statements (June 2025); HRANA; Israeli government figures; IAEA statements.

nodes.label: War with Iran
nodes.full: The United States and Israel began a campaign against Iran on 28 February 2026 during negotiations on its nuclear programme, killing Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and other leaders; Iran replied with missiles and drones on Israel, American bases and Gulf states and the closing of the Strait of Hormuz, and the war was marked by an April ceasefire mediated by Pakistan, failed talks, an American naval blockade of Iranian ports and renewed fighting, so that as of mid-October 2026 its end has not been settled; casualty figures differ widely by source and the Iranian government reported thousands of dead.
nodes.src: Wikipedia and Britannica entries "2026 Iran war" (accessed October 2026); AP and Reuters reports; Iran 1979–today folio.

nodes.label: PKK conflict
nodes.full: The armed struggle of the Kurdistan Workers' Party, begun in 1984 and having cost some 40,000 lives, with the destruction of villages in the 1990s, the capture of Abdullah Öcalan in 1999, the failed settlement process of 2013–2015 and operations across the borders in Iraq and Syria, was followed by a call by Öcalan on 27 February 2025 to dissolve the movement, the PKK's announcement of its dissolution on 12 May 2025 and a symbolic burning of weapons in July 2025, with the political and legal arrangements still under negotiation in 2026.
nodes.src: Turkey 1980–today folio; Öcalan statement (27 February 2025); PKK congress announcement (12 May 2025); Reuters and AP reports.

nodes.label: Oslo Accords
nodes.full: The Declaration of Principles signed on the White House lawn on 13 September 1993 by Yitzhak Rabin and Yasser Arafat, after secret talks in Norway, with mutual recognition of Israel and the PLO and an interim self-government for the Palestinians of the West Bank and Gaza, was followed by the Oslo II agreement of September 1995 dividing the West Bank into Areas A, B and C; the final status issues of Jerusalem, borders, refugees and settlements were never resolved, and the assassination of Rabin on 4 November 1995, by an Israeli opponent of the accords, and the later violence ended the process.
nodes.src: Declaration of Principles (13 September 1993); Interim Agreement (28 September 1995); Avi Shlaim, The Iron Wall (2000).

nodes.label: Iraqi constitution
nodes.full: The constitution approved by referendum on 15 October 2005, with some 79 per cent in favour though strongly opposed in the Sunni Arab provinces, made Iraq a federal and parliamentary republic with Islam as a source of legislation, recognised the Kurdistan Region and allowed provinces to form regions; the unresolved clauses on Kirkuk, oil and the division of powers have been disputes ever since, and a system of sectarian quotas (muhasasa) took shape in practice.
nodes.src: Constitution of Iraq (2005); Iraq 2003–today folio; Dodge 2012.

nodes.label: Egyptian constitutions
nodes.full: The constitution of December 2012, written by an Islamist-led assembly and approved by some 64 per cent on a low turnout, was suspended after Morsi's removal; the constitution of January 2014 was approved by about 98 per cent in a referendum which the Brotherhood boycotted, and the amendments of April 2019 extended the presidential term to six years, allowed Sisi to stay until 2030 and increased the role of the army and the president over the judiciary.
nodes.src: Constitution of Egypt (2012, 2014); referendum results (2019); Egypt 1952–today folio.

nodes.label: Turkish presidential system
nodes.full: A referendum under the state of emergency on 16 April 2017 approved by 51.4 per cent a package of eighteen amendments that replaced the parliamentary system with an executive presidency, abolishing the post of prime minister and giving the president powers to rule by decree, to appoint ministers and senior judges and to be a party leader; its supporters called it a guarantee of stability, its opponents a one-man regime, and observers of the Council of Europe criticised the unequal conditions of the campaign.
nodes.src: Supreme Election Council (16 April 2017); OSCE/PACE observation report (2017); Turkey 1980–today folio.

nodes.label: Syrian constitutional declaration
nodes.full: The Constitutional Declaration signed by interim president Ahmed al-Sharaa on 13 March 2025, a few days after the massacres on the coast, set a five-year transition, Islamic jurisprudence as the main source of legislation, a strong presidency and a people's assembly partly appointed by the president; the Kurdish-led authorities, the Druze and the Alawite leaders objected to its centralisation and the agreement on the integration of the Kurdish forces was repeatedly revised.
nodes.src: Constitutional Declaration (13 March 2025); UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria reports; Syria 1946–today folio.

nodes.label: International courts
nodes.full: The International Court of Justice in an advisory opinion of 9 July 2004 held the barrier in the West Bank contrary to international law, in July 2024 held the continued occupation unlawful and in 2024 heard the case brought by South Africa under the Genocide Convention, with provisional measures in January, March and May 2024; the International Criminal Court issued warrants in November 2024 against Netanyahu, Gallant and Hamas's Mohammed Deif; Israel rejects the jurisdiction and the allegations, and the United States does not recognise the ICC's jurisdiction.
nodes.src: ICJ advisory opinions (2004, 2024); ICJ South Africa v. Israel orders (2024); ICC Pre-Trial Chamber decisions (21 November 2024).

nodes.label: Political Islam
nodes.full: Islamist parties won elections: the AKP in Turkey (2002), Hamas in Palestine (2006), Ennahda in Tunisia (2011) and the Brotherhood's Freedom and Justice Party in Egypt, which gained 47 per cent of the seats in 2011–2012 and the presidency in June 2012, only to see the Egyptian experiment end in the removal of Morsi in 2013 and the Brotherhood's designation as a terrorist organisation; scholars still argue whether the 2013 failure was due to the movement's own errors, the old state's resistance or both.
nodes.src: Egypt 1952–today folio; Nathan Brown, When Victory Is Not an Option (2012); Olivier Roy, The Failure of Political Islam (1994).

nodes.label: Jihadism
nodes.full: The al-Qaeda movement of Osama bin Laden, which declared war on the United States in 1996 and carried out the attacks of 11 September 2001, was followed in Iraq by al-Zarqawi's group and the Islamic State, whose declaration of a caliphate in 2014 claimed political authority over all Muslims; the movements were rejected by almost all Muslim scholars and killed far more Muslims than others, and their attraction, which drew some 40,000 foreign recruits to Syria and Iraq by 2017, was a subject of debate.
nodes.src: Lawrence Wright, The Looming Tower (2006); Gerges 2016; The Soufan Center, Beyond the Caliphate (2017).

nodes.label: Sectarian conflict
nodes.full: The bombing of the al-Askari mosque at Samarra on 22 February 2006 began the Iraqi sectarian war of 2006–2008, with death squads, ethnic cleansing of neighbourhoods in Baghdad and more than a million displaced; the divide spread to Syria, Bahrain, Yemen and Lebanon and into the rivalry of Saudi Arabia and Iran, though historians note that political leaders turned identity into a weapon and that most communities had long lived together.
nodes.src: Vali Nasr, The Shia Revival (2006); Fanar Haddad, Sectarianism in Iraq (2011); Iraq 2003–today folio.

nodes.label: Jerusalem
nodes.full: The status of Jerusalem's Temple Mount, which Muslims call the Haram al-Sharif, with al-Aqsa and the Dome of the Rock, remained the most volatile question: Sharon's visit in September 2000 was the trigger of the intifada, the United States recognised Jerusalem as Israel's capital on 6 December 2017 and moved its embassy on 14 May 2018, Jordan's role as custodian was reaffirmed in 2013, and Israel's annexation of East Jerusalem in 1980 is not recognised by most states.
nodes.src: Jordan 1946–today and Israel 1948–today folios; UN Security Council resolutions 478 (1980) and 2334 (2016); UNGA resolution ES-10/19 (2017).

nodes.label: Christians of the East
nodes.full: Iraq's Christians, some 1.4 million in 2003 by commonly cited estimates, fell to a few hundred thousand or fewer after the church bombings of 2004–2010, the exodus from Mosul in July 2014 and the flight from the Nineveh plain; the Copts of Egypt suffered attacks on churches in 2011, 2016–2017 and later, and those of Syria and Palestine, who were a larger share in 1900, declined in numbers through emigration, in a region in which the Churches were among the oldest communities.
nodes.src: Iraq 2003–today folio; Pew Research Center estimates; Philip Jenkins, The Lost History of Christianity (2008).

nodes.label: Al Jazeera
nodes.full: Al Jazeera, launched in Doha on 1 November 1996 with funds from the Emir of Qatar and staff from the closed BBC Arabic television, broke the state monopoly of Arab news with live debate, coverage of the second intifada, Afghanistan and Iraq and, in 2011, of the uprisings; admired as a free voice and criticised as an instrument of Qatari policy, it spawned rivals such as al-Arabiya (2003) and made satellite television a public sphere.
nodes.src: Mohamed Zayani (ed.), The Al Jazeera Phenomenon (2005); Marc Lynch, Voices of the New Arab Public (2006); Qatar 1971–today folio.

nodes.label: Iranian cinema
nodes.full: Abbas Kiarostami's Taste of Cherry won the Palme d'Or at Cannes in 1997 and Asghar Farhadi's A Separation took the first Oscar for Iran for the best foreign-language film in 2012, followed by The Salesman in 2017, while Jafar Panahi, who had been banned from filmmaking and imprisoned, won the Palme d'Or in 2025 for It Was Just an Accident; the films, made under censorship, are known as portraits of ordinary people under pressure.
nodes.src: Hamid Dabashi, Close Up (2001); Cannes and Academy Awards records; Iran 1979–today folio.

nodes.label: Pamuk
nodes.full: Orhan Pamuk, the author of Snow (2002), My Name Is Red (1998) and the memoir Istanbul (2003), was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature on 12 October 2006, the first Turkish winner, after he had been prosecuted in 2005 under the law against insulting Turkishness for remarks on the killing of Armenians and Kurds; the prize made him a symbol both of the country's literary reach and of its limits on speech.
nodes.src: Nobel Foundation (2006); Pamuk, Istanbul: Memories and the City (2003); Turkey 1980–today folio.

nodes.label: Art of the squares
nodes.full: The revolutions of 2011 produced in Cairo's Mohamed Mahmoud Street and Tahrir Square a graffiti and street art of martyrs' portraits, satire and political slogans, songs such as Ramy Essam's Irhal (Leave) and the documentary The Square (2013), by Jehane Noujaim, and similar work in Tunis, Sanaa and Damascus, much of which was whitewashed by the authorities after 2013.
nodes.src: Mia Gröndahl, Revolution Graffiti (2012); Jehane Noujaim, The Square (2013); Egypt 1952–today folio.

nodes.label: Clash of civilizations
nodes.full: Samuel Huntington's essay The Clash of Civilizations? in Foreign Affairs (1993) and book (1996) argued that after the Cold War the main lines of conflict would be cultural, with Islam in particular on a bloody frontier; it was criticised by Edward Said and by scholars for its essentialism and answered by Khatami's proposal of a dialogue among civilizations, and it entered public debate again after 11 September 2001.
nodes.src: Samuel Huntington, The Clash of Civilizations and the Remaking of World Order (1996); Edward Said, The Clash of Ignorance (2001).

nodes.label: Arab Human Development Reports
nodes.full: The first Arab Human Development Report, prepared by Arab scholars for the United Nations Development Programme, identified three deficits in the region, of freedom, of knowledge and of women's empowerment, and its findings, of low translation rates, a weak research base and the lack of political rights, shaped debate on reform in the Arab world and were used by both governments and critics of the region's regimes.
nodes.src: UNDP, Arab Human Development Report 2002; Nader Fergany et al.

nodes.label: Iranian reformism
nodes.full: The election of Mohammad Khatami as president in May 1997 with some 70 per cent of the vote opened a period of reformist politics, with the thought of Abdolkarim Soroush on the plurality of religious understanding, the new press and his proposal of a dialogue among civilizations that the United Nations took up in 2001; the conservative institutions of the Guardian Council and the judiciary closed newspapers and disqualified candidates and the movement lost ground by 2005.
nodes.src: Abdolkarim Soroush, Reason, Freedom and Democracy in Islam (2000); Abrahamian 2008; Iran 1979–today folio.

nodes.label: Oil cycles
nodes.full: Oil prices that fell to below 12 dollars a barrel in 1998 rose to a record of some 147 dollars in July 2008, collapsed in the crash of 2008–2009 and again from 2014, fell briefly below zero for the American benchmark on 20 April 2020 in the pandemic and rose above 100 dollars in 2022 after the invasion of Ukraine, each swing sending the Gulf states' budgets, their investment funds and the remittance-dependent economies of the region through boom and austerity.
nodes.src: US Energy Information Administration data; Yergin, The Quest (2011); Saudi 1902–today folio.

nodes.label: Vision 2030
nodes.full: Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030, announced on 25 April 2016, aimed to reduce the economy's dependence on oil through the Public Investment Fund, the opening of tourism and entertainment and megaprojects such as NEOM; the partial listing of Saudi Aramco on the Riyadh exchange in December 2019, with some 25.6 billion dollars raised, was at the time the largest initial public offering, and the programme's targets, costs and realism are debated, with several projects scaled back in 2024–2025.
nodes.src: Saudi Vision 2030 document (2016); Aramco prospectus (2019); Saudi 1902–today folio.

nodes.label: Sanctions
nodes.full: The United Nations sanctions on Iraq from August 1990, which with the oil-for-food programme of 1996 lasted until 2003 and caused a collapse of living standards disputed in its mortality estimates; the American and European sanctions on Iran, intensified in 2010–2012 and after the American withdrawal from the nuclear deal in 2018; and the sanctions on Syria, including the Caesar Act of 2019, which the United States began to lift in 2025, show both the tool's use and its contested effects on civilians.
nodes.src: UN Security Council resolution 661 (1990); Joy Gordon, Invisible War (2010); US Treasury announcements (2025).

nodes.label: Currency crises
nodes.full: The Lebanese pound lost some 90 per cent of its value after 2019, in what the World Bank called one of the worst financial crises in the world since the middle of the nineteenth century; the Turkish lira lost most of its value from 2018 to 2023 as the central bank cut rates against inflation; and the Egyptian pound was floated in 2016 and devalued in 2022–2024, each with large losses to savings and wages.
nodes.src: World Bank, Lebanon Economic Monitor (2021); Turkish Statistical Institute and central bank data; Lebanon, Turkey and Egypt folios.

nodes.label: Social media
nodes.full: Facebook pages such as We Are All Khaled Said helped to call the demonstrations of 25 January 2011 in Egypt and Twitter and mobile video carried the Green Movement of Iran in 2009 and the protests of 2022, while governments learned to shut down the internet, as Egypt did on 28 January 2011 and Iran in 2019 and 2022, and to use the platforms for surveillance and propaganda; the technology gave the movements speed but not, as later events showed, durable organisation.
nodes.src: Zeynep Tufekci, Twitter and Tear Gas (2017); Philip Howard, The Digital Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy (2010); NetBlocks reports.

nodes.label: Nuclear programme
nodes.full: The revelation in August 2002 of the secret enrichment plant at Natanz and the heavy-water site at Arak began a dispute over whether Iran's programme was only civil, as Iran says, or a path to a weapon, as Israel and the Western states hold; the Stuxnet worm of 2010, the nuclear deal of 2015, the enrichment to 60 per cent purity after 2021 and the attacks of June 2025 on Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan are the stations of a programme whose present state and stock of enriched uranium are uncertain as of 2026.
nodes.src: IAEA Board reports (2003–2025); Iran 1979–today folio; David Sanger, Confront and Conceal (2012).

nodes.label: Missiles and drones
nodes.full: The Iron Dome system, first used in April 2011, together with David's Sling and Arrow, was built against the rockets and missiles of Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran, whose drones and missiles, such as the Shahed, were used by the Houthis, in Iraq and Syria, in the attack on Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq plant in September 2019 and in the war in Ukraine, while Turkey's Bayraktar drones were used in Syria, Libya and the Caucasus: cheap long-range weapons changed the region's balance of power.
nodes.src: Israel Ministry of Defense; Turkey 1980–today folio; reports on the Abqaiq attack (2019).

nodes.label: Madrid and the Arab Peace Initiative
nodes.full: The conference opened at Madrid on 30 October 1991 under American and Soviet auspices began direct talks of Israel with Syria, Lebanon and a joint Jordanian–Palestinian delegation, and was followed by Oslo, the Israel–Jordan treaty of 26 October 1994 and, at the Beirut summit of March 2002, the Arab Peace Initiative offering full normalisation in return for withdrawal to the lines of 1967 and a just solution of the refugee question, which Israel has not accepted as formulated.
nodes.src: Arab Peace Initiative (28 March 2002); Israel–Jordan Peace Treaty (26 October 1994); Shlaim 2000.

nodes.label: Nuclear deal
nodes.full: The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action of 14 July 2015, agreed by Iran with China, France, Germany, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States, limited Iran's enrichment and stockpile and subjected it to inspection in return for the lifting of nuclear sanctions; the United States withdrew from it on 8 May 2018 and reimposed sanctions, Iran stepped away from its limits from 2019 and the European parties triggered the return of United Nations sanctions in September 2025, which Iran, Russia and China hold to be invalid.
nodes.src: JCPOA (14 July 2015); UN Security Council resolution 2231 (2015); IAEA reports; Iran 1979–today folio.

nodes.label: Abraham Accords
nodes.full: The agreements signed on 15 September 2020 at the White House by Israel with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, followed by Morocco and Sudan in the same year, made them the first Arab states since Jordan in 1994 to normalise relations without the settlement of the Palestinian question, a departure from the Arab Peace Initiative's order of steps; Saudi Arabia has linked its own agreement to a path to a Palestinian state, and the Gaza war froze the process.
nodes.src: Abraham Accords (15 September 2020); Israel 1948–today folio; Bahrain and Qatar folios.

nodes.label: Beijing agreement
nodes.full: Saudi Arabia and Iran, which had cut relations in January 2016 after the storming of the Saudi embassy in Tehran following the execution of the Shia cleric Nimr al-Nimr, announced on 10 March 2023 in Beijing, with Chinese mediation, the restoration of relations and the reopening of embassies; the agreement lowered the temperature on Yemen and the Gulf but did not resolve the underlying rivalry, which was tested again by the Iran war of 2026.
nodes.src: Joint trilateral statement (10 March 2023); Saudi 1902–today and Iran 1979–today folios.

nodes.label: Astana format
nodes.full: Russia's intervention of 30 September 2015 on the side of Assad reversed his government's losses and was followed by the recapture of Aleppo in December 2016 and the Astana process of Russia, Iran and Turkey, which set up de-escalation zones and in 2020 the Idlib ceasefire; the arrangement, in which Turkey held the north and Iran the militias, held until the opposition offensive of late 2024, when Russia and Iran did not save the government.
nodes.src: Astana joint statements (2017–2024); Syria 1946–today folio; International Crisis Group reports.

nodes.label: Syrian refugees
nodes.full: By 2016 the United Nations counted some 5 million registered Syrian refugees, with about 3 million in Turkey (3.6 million at the peak), around a million in Lebanon and some 650,000 registered in Jordan, while in 2015 more than a million migrants reached Europe, Syrians the largest group among them, and some 6.7 million were displaced within Syria; after the fall of Assad in December 2024 hundreds of thousands, and by UNHCR counts over a million, returned in 2025 to a country with destroyed housing and services.
nodes.src: UNHCR Global Trends reports (2016–2025); Syria Regional Refugee Response portal; Syria 1946–today folio.

nodes.label: Water and drought
nodes.full: Dams in Turkey and Iran, falling rainfall and over-pumping brought the flow of the Tigris and Euphrates to historic lows, the drying of the marshes in southern Iraq, drought from 2007 to 2010 in Syria, which some scholars link to rural migration before 2011, though others dispute the causal claim, and severe water shortage in Iran's cities, including Tehran, in 2025; summer temperatures of over 50 degrees Celsius have become more common.
nodes.src: Colin Kelley et al., PNAS (2015); World Bank, Iraq Country Climate and Development Report (2022); Iran 1979–today folio.

nodes.label: Earthquakes
nodes.full: Two earthquakes of magnitude 7.8 and 7.5 on 6 February 2023 along the East Anatolian fault, with their epicentres near Kahramanmaraş, killed more than 50,000 people in Turkey and several thousand in northern Syria, where aid reached the opposition-held areas slowly across a war front, and destroyed or damaged hundreds of thousands of buildings; the quality of construction and the amnesties for illegal building became a political issue before the elections of May 2023.
nodes.src: AFAD and Turkish government reports (2023); UN OCHA; Turkey 1980–today folio.

nodes.label: Beirut explosion
nodes.full: The explosion on 4 August 2020 of some 2,750 tonnes of ammonium nitrate, which had been stored in the port warehouse for six years after being confiscated from a ship, killed more than 215 people, injured some 6,000 to 7,000 and left some 300,000 homeless; the judicial inquiry has been obstructed by political interference and, by reports to 2026, no senior official has been convicted.
nodes.src: Human Rights Watch, They Killed Us from the Inside (2021); Lebanon 1943–today folio.

nodes.label: COVID-19
nodes.full: Iran, where the first deaths were reported in Qom in February 2020, was among the early centres of the pandemic outside China and reported well over 100,000 deaths by official count, Turkey and Egypt tens of thousands each and the Gulf states relatively few; excess-mortality estimates by the World Health Organization and the Economist suggest that official figures were substantially understated in several countries, and the lockdowns hit the migrant workers, the tourist economies and the countries already in crisis such as Lebanon and Yemen.
nodes.src: World Health Organization, Global excess deaths estimates (2022); national health ministry reports; Iran 1979–today folio.

nodes.label: Women’s rights
nodes.full: Kuwaiti women won the vote and the right to stand in May 2005, Saudi women were permitted to drive in June 2018, and in Iran the death in custody on 16 September 2022 of Mahsa Amini, a young Kurdish woman arrested by the morality police for her hijab, began the Woman, Life, Freedom protests, in which hundreds were killed, thousands arrested and many women went without the compulsory headscarf; in each case the changes and the restrictions came from the same governments.
nodes.src: Kuwait 1961–today and Saudi 1902–today folios; UN fact-finding mission on Iran (2024); Iran 1979–today folio.

nodes.label: Yazidis
nodes.full: When Islamic State forces took Sinjar on 3 August 2014 they killed several thousand Yazidi men, enslaved some 6,000 women and children and drove some 200,000 to flee, many to Mount Sinjar; the United Nations commission of inquiry found in June 2016 that the acts amounted to genocide, the remains of mass graves are still being exhumed and thousands of the Yazidi captives were still missing at the end of the decade.
nodes.src: UN Human Rights Council, "They Came to Destroy" (A/HRC/32/CRP.2, 2016); Iraq 2003–today folio.

nodes.label: Hostages and displaced
nodes.full: In Israel the families of the hostages taken on 7 October, of whom some 250 were taken and who were released in exchanges in November 2023, January–March 2025 and October 2025, formed a mass movement and tens of thousands of residents were evacuated from the south and north; in Gaza, according to the United Nations, about 90 per cent of the population of some 2.1 million was displaced at least once, many repeatedly, with shortages of food and medicine and a famine declared by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification for Gaza City in August 2025, which Israel disputed.
nodes.src: UN OCHA reports; IPC Gaza analysis (22 August 2025); Israeli government statements; Hostages and Missing Families Forum.

nodes.label: Migrant workers
nodes.full: Migrant workers, from South Asia, the Philippines and East Africa, make up some 70 to 90 per cent of the population of Qatar, the Emirates and Kuwait; the sponsorship system kafala, restrictions on changing employer, unpaid wages and deaths on building sites, including the construction for the 2022 World Cup, brought the reforms of Qatar in 2017–2020, such as a minimum wage, and continued criticism that enforcement is weak and the numbers of deaths disputed.
nodes.src: Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch reports (2013–2022); Qatar 1971–today and Kuwait folios.

nodes.label: Protest generation
nodes.full: In October 2019 young people in Baghdad and southern Iraq took to the streets in the Tishreen protests against corruption, unemployment and the quota system, and some 600 or more were killed and thousands wounded by security forces and militias; in Lebanon the demonstrations of 17 October against a tax on messaging calls grew into a nationwide movement against the whole political class, and both movements led to the fall of the governments, but the system and its leaders remained.
nodes.src: UN Assistance Mission for Iraq reports (2020); Amnesty International, Iraq (2020); Lebanon 1943–today and Iraq 2003–today folios.

nodes.label: The Kurds
nodes.full: The Kurds, who gained a recognised region in Iraq in 2005, a de facto autonomous area (Rojava) in northeastern Syria from 2012, held an independence referendum in Iraqi Kurdistan on 25 September 2017, approved by about 93 per cent, which the central government answered by retaking Kirkuk in October; in Syria the autonomous administration's forces, after defeating the Islamic State, signed in 2025–2026 agreements on integration into the Syrian state, the terms and future of which are uncertain, and in Turkey the PKK's dissolution opened an unresolved question of rights.
nodes.src: Iraqi Kurdistan Region electoral commission (2017); Syria 1946–today and Turkey 1980–today folios; Reuters reports (2026).

nodes.label: The inheritance of the Cold War Near East
nodes.full: The oil states, the Arab republics, the Iranian revolution, the Lebanese war and the Arab–Israeli conflict of the years to 1990 set the problems that the post-Cold War period inherited.
nodes.src: background — see the Modern Near East 1945–1990 folio (modern-near-east-1945-1990)

nodes.label: The occupation of 1967
nodes.full: The conquest of the West Bank, Gaza, Sinai and the Golan Heights in June 1967 created the territorial questions that Oslo, the intifadas and the Gaza wars have centred on.
nodes.src: background — see the Israel 1948–today folio (israel-1948-today)
